An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Qatar warns of industrial catastrophe as Hormuz traffic falls to 10 a day
brief.h: Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman Mohammed Al-Ansari said reopening the Strait of Hormuz is now the priority if an "industrial catastrophe" is to be avoided, as Kpler data showed only about ten commodity ships a day crossing the strait over the past ten days - the lowest run since May - and Brent added 34 cents to $97.34 with WTI up 1.26 per cent at $92.63, after Iran threatened to retaliate against any new US strikes on its assets.
brief.t: The number that moved today is not the price, it is Goldman's assumption. The bank raised its December-2026 Brent forecast by $5 to $85 and its 2027 number to $80 explicitly because it now assumes Middle East shipping disruption runs into next year - the first time a major desk has written multi-year interdiction into a base case rather than a risk case. Read the two figures together and the market's actual view falls out: spot at $97 with an $85 forecast says traders expect the war premium to decay but the floor underneath it to sit permanently higher, which is the price signature of a chokepoint that stays expensive after it stops being dangerous. Qatar's intervention is the same story from the other end of the pipe - the world's second-largest LNG exporter ships every cargo through that strait and has no navy answer, so its only instrument is to make Washington's escort mission a Qatari priority in public.
brief.context: The rail is the 1980s tanker war, and its base rate is the discipline here: roughly 450 vessels were attacked across four years and the strait never closed - what moved was the premium, the flag and the convoy, and traffic recovered when underwriters requoted rather than when the shooting stopped. The deciding desk is therefore the reinsurance treaty behind the International Group's pooling arrangement, not CENTCOM, because cover is the gate on every sailing decision. Our published falsifier stands: transits back above twenty-five a day for a week WITH war-risk quotes under two per cent of hull value. Ten a day is the opposite of that, and it is now Kpler's number rather than ours.

angles.effect: gains by converting a commercial exposure into an allied obligation - saying the quiet part in public makes LNG escorting a stated US priority without Doha paying for a single hull or firing a shot.
gains the interdiction without owning it. Ten transits a day is a blockade result achieved by threat and premium; Tehran has still not formally closed anything and keeps the deniability.
gains a case for the escort mission but pays in pump prices into a midterm, and now faces a sell-side house telling clients the disruption is a 2027 fact rather than a 2026 event.

angles.party: Asian refiners and Japanese and Korean utilities
angles.effect: pay the freight and the LNG differential with no seat at any table where escorting, quoting or pricing is decided.
pay first and in cash, and have already pushed the exposure back onto owners through cancellation notices.

dec.kill: Kpler transits back above twenty-five a day for a full week with war-risk quotes under two per cent of hull value. That combination, not a ceasefire headline or a Qatari statement, is the observable.

consp.claim: That Saudi Arabia has already begun retaliating for a large overnight Houthi salvo - the circulating list has the Houthis hitting King Khalid Air Base at Khamis Mushait, Abha International Airport, an Aramco bulk plant at Abha and the Jizan refinery again, with Riyadh's answer said to be under way and no wire carrying it.
consp.spread: The running item list at the top of /pol/'s Persia-Israel general #2068, at 261 replies, fed by Telegram OSINT channels and reposted video.
consp.read: The mechanics are proven rather than imagined - the same two southern Saudi targets were struck in July and Jizan has been hit twice in a month - which is exactly why the template is also easy to copy without anything new happening. The checkable part is airspace: a NOTAM closing Abha or Khamis Mushait, or a Saudi defence ministry statement, would convert this from a board list into a fact, and its absence eight hours in is the argument against it.

brief.head: Russia hits Kyiv again as the Witkoff pause expires with no deal
brief.h: Russian drones struck the Boryspil and Fastiv districts early Tuesday, Kyiv's military administration declared an air alert and TASS confirmed that the three-day halt Putin had ordered to cover the Witkoff and Kushner shuttle through Moscow and Kyiv had run out; Witkoff talks of reviving three-way talks, Zelensky told the envoys the war will likely "continue in winter", and Ukraine's prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko resigned the same night after anti-corruption detectives searched his offices over a money-laundering scheme they say was run by one of his own officials.
brief.t: A pause that expires exactly on schedule is not a failed ceasefire, it is a completed transaction. Putin gave up nothing - three nights of not striking one city - and bought two things with it: a photograph of American envoys leaving Moscow claiming progress, and a live demonstration to Kyiv that the tap is his to open and close on a calendar. The tell is that what Witkoff came back with is a scheduling ambition with no date, no city and no jointly acknowledged text, which is the cheapest possible output of a summit shuttle. Underneath it, the Kravchenko resignation matters more than the drones: Ukraine's leverage in any trilateral rests on being the party whose institutions are worth guaranteeing, and a chief prosecutor leaving over a laundering scheme inside his own office is a direct debit against that.
brief.context: The rail is the envoy-window pause, a recurring instrument in this war since 2022 - Moscow grants a dated quiet coinciding with a visit, lets it lapse, and pockets the process credit. The base rate is unkind: no such pause has yet converted into a demarcation line, a named monitor or a guarantor list. The deciding desk is not the podium but whoever in the Kremlin controls the Geran launch schedule, because a pause that can be switched on and off in 72-hour blocks is a coercive instrument, not a concession. What would change the read is a jointly acknowledged text - a date, a city, a named guarantor - which is exactly the falsifier already published against this board's Kyiv-pause clock.

angles.effect: gain a deliverable that costs the United States nothing and can be described as momentum - progress towards scheduling a trilateral is a claim about a calendar, not about terms.
gains a free demonstration of control over escalation and a reputational credit for restraint, having conceded no territory, no line and no monitor, and resumes on the hour the window closes.

pays. He is pushed towards a process he cannot decline while his own prosecutorial apparatus is publicly compromised, which weakens the argument that Ukrainian institutions are the thing being guaranteed.
pay the actual cost of the instrument - three nights of sleep in exchange for the fourth night's drones, with the schedule set elsewhere.

dec.kill: A jointly acknowledged trilateral text with a date, a city and a named guarantor before the end of September. Absent that, tonight's resumption scores the peace-track read as talk rather than movement.

consp.claim: That Ukraine's security services are now in open factional conflict and that the anti-corruption raids are the visible edge of a succession fight timed to the peace track - the circulating item list has SBU and HUR personnel shooting at each other on the streets of Kyiv, an assassination attempt on a Russian long-range aviation commander, and Russia "returning to communism" by seizing private companies designated extremist.
consp.spread: The pinned item list of /pol/'s Ukraine Happening General #20120 at 187 replies, cross-posted into the rival /chug/ thread which pre-emptively labels any Kyiv-sourced item fake.
consp.read: This is the standard wartime frame in which every corruption case is read as an intelligence operation rather than a corruption case, and the kernel is real - Zelensky did publicly call an SBU-HUR confrontation a disgrace, and Kravchenko's resignation letter itself uses the language of political confrontation. What the boards add is the causal claim, that Washington is arranging a replacement, and there is nothing under that but sequence.

brief.head: Canada's tariffs on 700 US goods bite as Trump targets Bombardier
brief.h: Ottawa's retaliation took effect Tuesday - more than 700 American products facing duties of 15, 25 or 50 per cent, steel and aluminium doubled to 50, on a list finance minister Francois-Philippe Champagne published in a near-hundred-page schedule answering the roughly C$27.6bn of Canadian exports hit by Washington on 22 August - and Trump replied by posting "No more selling Bombardier in the United States!" and telling Canada that if it wants the US market it must build there and "stop treating America like a 'piggybank'".
brief.t: There is no rail under the Bombardier threat, and that is the point worth holding. Aircraft are certified by the FAA, not the White House, and there is no statute that lets a president bar a foreign manufacturer's sales by announcement - so the instrument here is not law, it is uncertainty priced into a fleet buyer's order book. Bombardier's own defence explains why executing it would be expensive: the company says more than half its revenue is American, built with parts from roughly 2,800 US suppliers across 47 states, which means a sales ban is a tariff on those 2,800 firms with extra steps. Follow the same logic through Carney's list and you see a mirror-image discipline - Ottawa exempted goods that comply with the USMCA and aimed at those that do not, which keeps the treaty alive while making the pain domestic and visible in American districts.
brief.context: The rail is the 2017 CSeries case, and it is the base rate that should govern this: Boeing complained, Commerce slapped roughly 300 per cent duties on Bombardier's jets, and the US International Trade Commission threw the whole thing out unanimously the following January because no American injury could be shown. Aerospace is the sector where integrated supply chains most reliably defeat trade coercion, and it is the sector Trump has chosen. The deciding desks are Commerce, the ITC and the FAA - none of them the podium - and the observable is procedural, not rhetorical. Carney suspended negotiations outright late last month, so the near-term path is escalation by schedule rather than by talks.

angles.effect: gains a costless pre-midterm demonstration of leverage over a partner most voters assume is compliant, at no fiscal cost while the threat stays a post.
gains a domestic rally and a narrowed, legally defensible list - USMCA-compliant goods spared - which lets him escalate while keeping the treaty argument on his side.

angles.party: Bombardier and its US supply chain
angles.effect: pay the uncertainty immediately in order timing and financing costs; roughly 2,800 American supplier firms in 47 states carry the exposure whether or not the ban is ever attempted.
pay through 50 per cent steel and aluminium duties that pass into construction, appliances and vehicles, and through the 15 to 50 per cent Canadian levies on smartphones, furniture, tools and food.

dec.kill: A Federal Register notice, a Commerce initiation or an FAA action naming Bombardier. Until one of those exists, this is a social-media post with a tariff schedule standing behind it, and should be read as the schedule rather than the post.

consp.claim: That Canada is being deliberately run into the ground and that the tariff fight is cover for an eventual absorption - the load-bearing exhibit circulating is a chart showing Canadian GDP per capita tracking the United States until 2014 and diverging sharply afterwards, pinned entirely on the immigration intake that ramped in the same year.
consp.spread: A 165-reply /pol/ thread titled CANADA IS COLLAPSING, recirculated in the Trump general and on X.
consp.read: The macro kernel is real and uncontroversial among economists - Canadian real GDP per capita has genuinely stagnated against the US since roughly 2015, driven by weak business investment and productivity as well as fast population growth. The persuasion move layered on top is single-cause attribution: one visible variable is selected from several, a post-2014 correlation is presented as the whole mechanism, and an ethnic-scapegoat narrative naming South Asian migrants is circulating attached to it, which is where the thread stops being an economic argument.

brief.head: Yen tops its July intervention peak as carry traders bail out
brief.h: The yen reached 153.53 to the dollar in Tokyo morning trade, its strongest since February and through the level Japan's July intervention bought, after a 1.2 per cent jump in Monday's thin US-holiday session left it nearly 4 per cent firmer than the 160 it traded at early last week; finance minister Katayama said Tokyo and Washington remain aligned on FX policy to foster stable markets, Japan revised up second-quarter GDP on capital spending, and the dollar sat subdued ahead of this week's CPI print.
brief.t: A four per cent move in the world's funding currency inside a week is not a Japanese story, it is a leverage story. The yen is what levered positions everywhere are borrowed in, so when it appreciates this fast the people selling are not expressing a view on Japan - they are being forced to close trades in everything else to buy back the borrow, which is why yen spikes historically arrive with equity drawdowns attached rather than after them. Reuters names the drivers as faster BoJ tightening bets, Japanese investors repatriating funds, and US political pressure, and the important word is repatriation: that is Japanese money coming home out of foreign bonds, which is a Treasury demand question as much as a currency one. Katayama's line about alignment is the part to read twice - Tokyo is getting a stronger yen without spending a single reserve dollar, so the market is doing the intervention for free.
brief.context: The rail is the carry unwind, and there are two clean precedents to size it against: October 1998, when the yen moved violently in days as LTCM-era positions were closed, and August 2024, when a much smaller BoJ surprise took global equities down inside 72 hours. Both needed two legs - a hawkish Tokyo and a dovish repricing of the Fed - and only the first leg is currently in place, which is why this board holds the full-unwind forecast at 29 rather than 40. The deciding desks are the MoF's currency bureau and the BoJ, with the FOMC on the 16th and the BoJ on the 18th two days apart. What kills it is a Fed that stays hawkish into a yen that has already run.

angles.effect: gains the outcome it paid for in July without paying again - a stronger yen delivered by positioning rather than reserves, and a verbal alignment with Washington that costs nothing to assert.

angles.party: Japanese exporters and the equity market
angles.effect: pay. Every yen of appreciation is translated earnings removed from the index that Japanese household savings are concentrated in.

angles.party: Levered carry holders and emerging-market borrowers
angles.effect: pay first and involuntarily - the borrow they are short is appreciating, and the assets they bought with it are what has to be sold to cover.
gains a weaker dollar it has publicly wanted, and pays if Japanese repatriation persists, because Japanese institutions are among the largest private holders of US government debt.

dec.kill: A BoJ hold on 18 September together with a hawkish Fed on the 16th, and the yen back through 158. That combination would mark this as positioning noise rather than the first leg of an unwind.

consp.claim: That the yen move is an engineered American operation rather than a Japanese one - the circulating version has the Treasury quietly buying yen and expanding buybacks while the Fed is briefed never to actually hike, with the strong yen a deliberate device to devalue the dollar and cheapen the debt service, and a parallel thread arguing foreign governments are pulling gold out of US vaults and foreign pensions are exiting US assets ahead of it.
consp.spread: Several /biz/ threads including a rugged-yen thread at 63 replies and a widely-read post laying out the Treasury-buys-yen sequence, plus a de-dollarisation thread on gold repatriation.
consp.read: This maps onto the Plaza Accord frame, which is the strongest available precedent for the claim - in 1985 the US genuinely did organise a coordinated dollar devaluation against the yen, so the mechanism is not invented. The checkable parts are public and currently do not support it: intervention shows up in the finance ministry's monthly operations data and in the US Treasury's TIC report, and the July operation was disclosed. The unfalsifiable part, and the reason to grade it as narrative, is that the thesis reads both a Fed hike and a Fed hold as confirmation.

brief.head: Merz doubles down on reforms after AfD landslide in Saxony-Anhalt
brief.h: The AfD took about 43.9 per cent in Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt vote and 39 of the Landtag's 83 seats - three short of a majority - against 17.2 per cent for Merz's CDU; the chancellor said his party was deeply shocked by "the most serious election defeat that the CDU has had for years, for decades", insisted "giving up is not an option for me" and confirmed he will press on with the unpopular economic reforms, while CDU general secretary Franziska Hoppermann ruled out any cooperation on the grounds that the AfD is a right-wing extremist party.
brief.t: The firewall has stopped being a moral position and become an arithmetic one, and that is the change tonight. Thirty-nine seats out of eighty-three means every remaining party in the chamber must combine to produce a government, which is to say the exclusion of the largest party can now only be enforced by building precisely the broad, ideologically incoherent coalition that generates the next AfD vote. Merz's answer - press on with unpopular reforms - is coherent only if the AfD vote is protest against economic drift rather than against the governing class as such; if it is the second, the reforms are the fuel. Note where the constraint sits: he cannot deal with the AfD without splitting his own party and forfeiting his coalition, and he cannot deliver growth before 20 September. He is boxed, and the boxing predicts the behaviour better than the man does.

lesson: Today's lesson is a media-literacy one, because the German result is going to be described to you in two ways that are both technically about the same number. When the AfD co-leader said the firewall had been DEFINITIVELY REJECTED BY THE VOTERS, watch the move: a plurality is being converted into a mandate. The party won 43.9 per cent, which is a genuinely large and genuinely democratic result - do not let anyone talk you out of that - but 43.9 per cent is not a majority of voters rejecting anything, and turnout rose from about 60 to about 80 per cent, meaning more people voted for EVERYONE. William Riker called this heresthetic: you win not by changing minds but by changing what the vote is understood to be ABOUT, and 'the voters rejected the firewall' redefines a seat count as a referendum on a norm. The counter-technique arrived the same night from the other direction - DW's fact-checkers documented fraud and vote-rigging claims spreading through the Matryoshka network, the Russian-linked operation that has targeted German elections before, which is Paul and Matthews' firehose of falsehood: not one persuasive lie but many cheap ones, fast, so that the cost of checking exceeds the cost of believing. What both techniques exploit is that you want a simple story about what a number MEANS. So here is the discipline, and it is boring on purpose: the honest test of 'the firewall was rejected' is not rhetoric, it is whether the firewall parties lost seats on net and whether any of them actually changes position in the coalition talks that start now. That is an observable with a date on it, and it is why this board raised its AfD Minister-President question to 23 per cent on the ballot ARITHMETIC rather than on the mood.

quiz.q: The AfD won 39 of 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt and every other party refuses to govern with it. Why does the brief still call an AfD Minister-President arithmetically possible?
options: Because the AfD can appoint a Minister-President directly once it wins the most votes
Because a third ballot is decided by a simple majority of votes cast, so abstentions can let 39 beat a divided 39
Because the federal chancellor can install a Land government when talks fail
Because the firewall is a law and laws can be repealed by a plurality
quiz.why: A cordon sanitaire is a coalition instrument. It denies a party partners; it does nothing about a ballot rule. quiz.q: Iran says its new restricted zone will begin at the US Navy blockade line, and that ships entering will be put on a sanctions list. What does the brief say that choice of penalty reveals?

That the zone is a bluff with no enforcement behind it
That Iran intends to seize every vessel that enters
quiz.why: Guns are expensive and reversible; a registry is cheap and permanent. quiz.q: Ship fuel is short while refineries are running hard. What is the mechanism the brief names?
options: Refineries are being sabotaged, so total output has collapsed
A record diesel crack makes it more profitable to squeeze every barrel into diesel, so the cheapest product in the barrel stops being made
Shipping demand has surged beyond any possible supply
Sanctions forbid the sale of marine fuel to commercial vessels
quiz.why: A barrel is a menu, not a single product. When the spread between crude and diesel hits records, the refiner reconfigures toward diesel and residual fuel oil - what ships burn - becomes the casualty. That is why the shortage shows up as a freight cost rather than as an empty pump.

quiz.q: The US Treasury joined a foreign currency intervention and pushed the Fed to widen the FIMA repo facility. What does FIMA actually let Japan do?

Borrow dollars against its Treasury holdings instead of selling them
Buy US Treasuries at a discount to the market
Convert its reserves into gold held at the New York Fed
quiz.why: The whole point is to prevent a forced seller. If Tokyo liquidates Treasuries to buy yen, it pushes up the yield on the debt Washington has to roll - so the US built a valve that lets an ally raise dollars without dumping the collateral. Published plumbing, not a secret favour, but it exists because the dependency runs both ways.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. After the Saxony-Anhalt result, an AfD co-leader said the firewall had been definitively rejected by the voters. Which observable best tests that CLAIM?

Whether commentators say the firewall is finished
Whether turnout rose compared with the previous election

Turnout rose from about 60 to about 80 per cent, which means more people voted for everyone. The honest test is behavioural on both sides: did the firewall bloc shrink in net seats, and does any of its members break? A plurality of 44 per cent is a genuinely large mandate and should not be dismissed - it is simply not the same proposition as a rejected firewall.

plumbing.read: The plumbing story today is not the oil price, it is who paid for Japan's currency defence. Tokyo spent a record 15.4 trillion yen, about $98.6bn, in the month to 26 August, and Bloomberg now reports it likely funded part of that by selling US Treasuries. That is the mechanism this board has been describing in the abstract, arriving as a print: a foreign official holder liquidating reserve assets pushes up the yield on the very instrument the US must roll, at the exact moment the ten-year sits at 4.77 per cent and the thirty-year at 5.25. Washington saw it coming. The reason the US Treasury joined a currency intervention at all - an almost unheard-of act - and the reason Bessent pushed the Fed to widen the FIMA repo facility, is that FIMA lets a foreign central bank borrow dollars AGAINST its Treasuries instead of selling them. Read that as what it is: a plumbing valve built to stop an ally from becoming a forced seller of American debt. It is not a secret bailout, it is published infrastructure - but the fact that it had to be widened tells you the balance-of-financial-terror is being actively managed rather than merely observed. sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
